Given the HTML below, use classList to: (1) add class 'active' to the button, (2) toggle the 'hidden' class on the alert box (to show it), (3) check if the alert box contains 'hidden' and log the result.
Why is `classList.add('active')` preferred over `element.className = 'active'`? Give a concrete scenario where using className directly would cause a problem.
questions.sample_answer: `classList.add('active')` adds the class to the existing class list without removing other classes. `element.className = 'active'` replaces the entire class attribute with just 'active', removing all previously applied classes. Concrete scenario: a button has `class="btn btn-primary"`. After the user clicks, you want to add 'active' to show it's selected. If you use `className = 'active'`, the button loses 'btn' and 'btn-primary', breaking its appearance completely. With `classList.add('active')`, it becomes `btn btn-primary active` — all classes preserved.

Given the HTML below, use querySelectorAll to select all course cards. Convert the NodeList to an array with Array.from, then use filter to keep only cards whose price paragraph contains '₦10' (use textContent and includes). Log the count of filtered cards.
Explain what a NodeList is and how it differs from a JavaScript array. Give two operations that work on both, and two that only work on arrays.
questions.sample_answer: A NodeList is a collection of DOM nodes returned by `querySelectorAll`. It is array-like but is not a JavaScript array — it is its own object type with its own prototype. Operations that work on both: length property (both have it), index access with [n] (both support it), forEach (NodeList has its own forEach). Operations that only work on arrays: map, filter, reduce, find, sort — these are Array.prototype methods and are not available on NodeList. To use them, convert with `Array.from(nodeList)` or `[...nodeList]`, which creates a real array from the NodeList's elements.

Given the HTML below, use querySelector to select the nested `.card-title` inside `.course-card`, then update its textContent. Also use setAttribute to set the card's `data-status` attribute to 'enrolled'. Log the updated title and the attribute value.
Why does placing a `<script>` tag at the bottom of `<body>` prevent a common DOM error? What error occurs if the script runs too early, and what is a modern alternative to bottom placement?
questions.sample_answer: HTML is parsed top-to-bottom. If a `<script>` is in the `<head>` or before body elements, it runs before those elements exist in the DOM. Any call like `document.getElementById('title')` returns `null` because the element hasn't been parsed yet. Calling a property on null — `null.textContent` — throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`. Bottom placement works because by the time the script runs, all HTML above it (the entire body) has been parsed and all elements exist. The modern alternative is the `defer` attribute on the script tag: `<script src='script.js' defer></script>`. A deferred script is downloaded in parallel but executes only after the full HTML document is parsed, regardless of where the script tag appears.

Describe the DOM tree structure using the terms: document, root, node, parent, child, sibling. Then explain what the `document` object is in JavaScript and how it is used to access page elements.
questions.sample_answer:
The DOM is a tree data structure. `document` is the root node — the top-level entry point from which the entire tree is accessible. Every HTML element becomes a node in the tree. A parent node is one that directly contains other nodes — `body` is the parent of `h1`. A child node is directly inside another node — `h1` is a child of `body`. Sibling nodes share the same parent — two `

` tags inside the same `

` are siblings. In JavaScript, `document` is a global object automatically available in the browser environment. It represents the entire HTML page and provides methods to access and modify its elements: `document.getElementById`, `document.querySelector`, `document.querySelectorAll`. It also has properties like `document.title` (the page title) and `document.body` (the body element). All DOM interaction starts from `document`.
